title: CoRGi: Content-Rich Graph Neural Networks with Attention

problem.claim: Graph representations and conventional GNN processing can fail to preserve rich information contained within graph nodes, such as textual content.

gap.claim: Existing approaches either ignore node content or summarize it into a single vector before GNN processing, without modeling the content in the context of neighboring nodes.

contributions.claim: CoRGi is a graph neural network that considers rich node data in the context of neighboring nodes.
CoRGi incorporates a personalized attention mechanism over each node's content into message passing.
CoRGi assigns user-item-specific attention scores to words appearing in an item's content.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report evaluating CoRGi on two edge-value prediction tasks.
The authors report that CoRGi makes better edge-value predictions than existing methods, especially in sparse graph regions.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph representations model domains as entities and relations but may omit rich information.
Node text can be important, yet conventional GNN processing ignores it or compresses it into one initialization vector.
CoRGi incorporates neighboring context and personalized word-level attention into message passing.
The authors report improved edge-value prediction on two tasks, particularly in sparse graph regions.

source_observation.claim: Node content can provide rich information that is lost when represented only as a graph structure or a single initialization vector.

interpretation.claim: When graph nodes contain structured or textual attributes, preserving content during neighborhood aggregation may improve predictions.

application.claim: Use content-aware, neighbor-conditioned attention for graph prediction tasks involving rich node attributes.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this approach improves all graph tasks or all graph density regimes.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the two edge-value prediction datasets or task details.
The abstract does not identify the baselines, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the attention architecture or training procedure.
